extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; readers of Montaigne; those interested in medicine, ethics, and philosophy (early modern audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern philosophical essay critiquing physicians, medical practice, and attitudes toward pain and death; offers prescriptive judgments about how patients and medicine ought to behave. Extracts standards for evaluating medical practice and conduct from Montaigne's prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should govern inward state, not external appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why should philosophy, which only has respect to life and effects, trouble itself about these external appearances? ... She forms us for ourselves, not for others; to be, not to seem; let her be satisfied with governing our understanding...","
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow ordinary bodily expressions (sighs, sobs, palpitations, turning pale) provided the courage is undaunted and tones are not expressive of despair. Philosophy's aim is to maintain the soul's understanding and composure rather than enforce ceremonial exterior decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit natural vocal expressions of pain so long as they do not express despair
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let her allow this vocal frailty to disease... provided the courage be undaunted, and the tones not expressive of despair, let her be satisfied. What matter the wringing of our hands, if we do not wring our thoughts?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require exact composedness in extreme suffering; if complaining or outcries relieve the body, they should not be forcibly suppressed. Epicurus even advises groaning in torments as a bodily relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain courage and rational capacity under suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul should be "in a condition to know itself, and to follow its accustomed way, contending with, and enduring, not meanly truckling under pain; moved and heated, not subdued and conquered,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a good patient by the preservation of rational discourse and understanding during pain — temporary interruptions are acceptable, but the mind must remain capable of thought and speech to some degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the mind by meditation to anticipate suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: "No new shape of suffering can arise new or unexpected; I have anticipated all, and acted them over beforehand in my mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipatory reflection on possible ailments reduces alarm and keeps the mind upright during sudden or severe attacks; the practice of mentally rehearsing misfortunes is recommended as a remedy to fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value experience and natural living over routine medical intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: "Physic is grounded upon experience and examples... I see no people so soon sick, and so long before they are well, as those who take much physic... The common people live well enough without it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate medicine by its net effect on life-span and wellbeing in practice; recognize that cultures and individuals have long thrived without physicians, and overreliance on medical prescriptions can corrupt health and shorten wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purging except in the extremest necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing Plato: "of three sorts of motions which are natural to us, purging is the worst, and that no man, unless he be a fool, ought to take anything to that purpose but in the extremest necessity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purgative treatments as dangerous and only employ them when absolutely necessary; unnecessary evacuations often harm constitution and provide no real benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer surgical certainty and specialization where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: "I conclude surgery to be much more certain, by reason that it sees and feels what it does, and so goes less upon conjecture... The Egyptians had reason to reject this general trade of physician, and to divide the profession: to each disease, to each part of the body, its particular workman."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor interventions grounded in direct observation (surgery) and a division of medical labor (specialists for particular organs or diseases) rather than a single generalist claiming authority over all ailments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of physicians' claims, secrecy, and profit-driven narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians "attribute to themselves" all happy outcomes, palliate their own errors with trivial excuses, and often disagree publicly; "they more consider their own reputation, and consequently their profit, than their patient's interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge physicians on transparency, consistency, and avoidance of self-serving explanations. Beware that medical success is often retroactively claimed and failures blamed on patients or extraneous causes; require accountability and clear causal reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject magical, occult, or fantastical remedies and rituals
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors' remedies described as: "the left foot of a tortoise, the urine of a lizard, the dung of an elephant... the excrement of rats beaten to powder," and odd rules about days, numbers, and hours of gathering simples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify such remedies as superstition rather than science; do not grant credibility to treatments whose selection rests on occult properties, numerology, or ritual timing rather than observable efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question the plausibility of mixed medicines claiming multiple targeted virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: "They will needs persuade us, that of their ingredients one will heat the stomach and the other will cool the liver... Of all this bundle of things having mixed up a potion, is it not a kind of madness to imagine or to hope that these differing virtues should separate themselves from one another in this mixture and confusion?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate compound medicines critically for interaction, loss of efficacy, and internal contradiction in claimed effects; be wary of trusting complex potions to perform many precise, divergent physiological tasks.
